onb.medida_simulada_la_produce: Simulated measurement (produced by the bench model)
onb.potencia_de_la_luz: Power of sunlight per unit area, in W/m². A module produces more the more irradiance it receives on its plane.
onb.luz_total_sobre_una: Total light on a horizontal surface: direct + diffuse. It is measured by the pyranometer (here, its simulated value).
onb.luz_que_llega_en: Light arriving in a straight line from the solar disc, measured perpendicular to the rays. Here it is a value derived from the model (pvlib), not an independent measurement by the pyranometer.
onb.luz_dispersada_por_el: Light scattered by the sky and the clouds. It is also a value derived from the model (pvlib).
onb.irradiancia_sobre_la_superficie: Irradiance on the tilted surface of the module; it is the one that matters for its power and it differs from GHI.
onb.direccion_hacia_la_que: Direction the panel faces, measured from north, in degrees: 90° east, 180° south, 270° west. The authorised range of the tracker is 90°–270°.
onb.angulo_del_panel_respecto: Angle of the panel with respect to the horizontal: 0° flat, 90° vertical. Authorised range 0°–90°.
onb.angulo_entre_la_normal: Angle between the panel normal and the solar ray. At 0° the Sun hits head-on and the panel collects the most; it grows as they become misaligned.
onb.modo_de_carga_que: Load mode that looks for the maximum power point of the I‑V curve to extract as much power as possible.
onb.punto_de_la_curva: Point of the curve where V·I is maximum (the “knee”). Its voltage is Vmp and its current Imp; here it is computed with the model.
onb.tension_maxima_del_modulo: Maximum voltage of the module when no current flows.
onb.corriente_maxima_del_modulo: Maximum current of the module when the voltage is zero; it grows almost linearly with irradiance.
onb.temperatura_de_las_celdas: Temperature of the module cells (simulator thermal model). As it rises, voltage and power drop.

labels.modulo_comercial_de_500: Commercial module of ~500 Wp at a fixed tilt (≈ latitude), facing south. It is the reference the moving module is compared against: any energy difference is due to orientation and tracking.
labels.modulo_identico_al_a: Module identical to A on a two-axis tracker with position feedback. It can work with both axes, lock one (azimuth or tilt practice), or follow the Sun astronomically or by sensors.
labels.mide_la_irradiancia_en: Measures irradiance in the same plane as the module (W/m²). It allows a fair comparison between modules, because each one receives a different irradiance depending on its orientation.
labels.igual_que_el_del: Same as module A's but mounted on the moving part: it tilts together with the panel and keeps measuring in its plane.
labels.mide_la_irradiancia_global: Measures global horizontal irradiance (GHI). It serves as a weather reference and, compared with the plane sensors, helps detect clouds or soiling. DNI and DHI are NOT measured by this sensor: they are values derived from the simulator model.
labels.velocidad_y_direccion_del: Wind speed and direction. In strong gusts the local controller moves the tracker to the safe position (horizontal) to protect the structure.
labels.sensor_protegido_por_un: Sensor protected by a stacked-plate radiation shield so that the Sun does not heat the reading. Ambient temperature determines how much the module heats up.
labels.registra_la_lluvia_acumulada: Records accumulated rainfall. It is used to interpret irradiance drops and as support for safety decisions.
labels.impone_el_punto_de: Imposes the operating point on each module (voltage, resistance, short circuit or maximum power point tracking) and allows automatic sweeps to obtain the I-V curve. The states are predefined and limited by the system.
labels.aloja_el_ni_cdaq: Houses the NI cDAQ-9184 with LabVIEW 2016 (to be confirmed in the inventory), the local controller, drivers and relays, and the DC protections. The critical safety limits live here and cannot be changed from the web.
labels.corta_la_energia_de: Cuts power to the motors and disconnects the load. It can only be reset on site with the key. Click the red button to trigger it (in the real practice only on-site staff would do so).
labels.permite_verificar_visualmente_el: Lets you visually verify the state of the test bench during the session. Click "View camera" to see its simulated image.
labels.apunta_al_modulo_movil: Points at the moving module: it is used to confirm with the image the movement reported by the telemetry.
labels.motorreductor_con_realimentacion_: Gearmotor with position feedback. Authorised range 90° to 270° (east–south–west) with hardware and software limit switches.
labels.actuador_lineal_que_inclina: Linear actuator that tilts the panel from 0° (horizontal, safe position) to 90°. With the azimuth axis locked, the tilt practice is carried out.
labels.transductores_aislados_de_tension: Isolated voltage and current transducers. Power and energy of the module are calculated from them.
labels.misma_instrumentacion_que_el: Same instrumentation as module A, synchronised with it so that power and energy can be compared.

prac.revisa_las_condiciones_abre: Check the conditions: open the pyranometer and the anemometer (click their labels) and confirm that the plane-of-array irradiance of module A (POA) exceeds 600 W/m² and that the wind is below 8 m/s.
prac.una_curva_i_v: An I‑V curve is only comparable if the irradiance is stable and sufficient. POA is the irradiance on the module's tilted plane (different from the horizontal GHI).
prac.ahora_poa_a_w: Now: POA A = {fmt} W/m² (you need > 600) · wind = {fmt2} m/s (you need < 8)

prac.verifica_el_banco_con: Check the test bench with IP camera 1: press "Camera 1", observe, and then leave the camera ("Exit camera" button) to return to the overview.
prac.antes_de_operar_se: Before operating, you confirm by image that the bench is clear and in a safe condition. Entering and leaving the camera are both counted.
prac.pon_la_carga_en: Set the load to OPEN CIRCUIT for at least 3 s and observe the Voc of each module.
prac.voc_es_la_tension: Voc is the maximum voltage: the current is zero and there is no power.
prac.pasa_a_cortocircuito_controlado: Switch to controlled SHORT CIRCUIT for at least 3 s and observe Isc.
prac.isc_es_la_corriente: Isc is the maximum current: the voltage is zero and there is no power either.
prac.lanza_el_barrido_i: Start the automatic I‑V sweep (10 s) and wait for it to finish completely.
prac.la_carga_recorre_la: The load sweeps the voltage from 0 to Voc and records I at each point. The irradiance must remain constant. An interrupted sweep does not count.
prac.aun_no_hay_un: There is no complete sweep yet.
prac.abre_la_pestana_i: Open the I‑V / P‑V tab and locate the maximum power point (◆).
prac.el_mpp_esta_en: The MPP is at the "knee" of the curve: there the V·I product is maximum. The dotted curve is the one calculated now; the dots are the recorded sweep.
prac.a_que_fraccion_de: At what fraction of Voc (Vmp/Voc) is the maximum power point, and why is the power zero at Voc and at Isc?
prac.vmp_voc_vmp_v: Vmp/Voc ≈ {fmt} (Vmp {fmt2} V, Voc {fmt3} V, values calculated now). At Voc I = 0 and at Isc V = 0, so P = V·I = 0. Fill factor FF = Pmp/(Voc·Isc) ≈ {v}.
prac.isc_crece_casi_linealmente: Isc grows almost linearly with irradiance; Voc varies only logarithmically and decreases with temperature.
prac.barrido_interrumpido_se_conservaron: Sweep interrupted ({cause}). {length} points were kept, but it does not count: repeat it.

prac.cuantificar_cuanta_potencia_se: Quantify how much power is gained or lost when changing azimuth and tilt, by comparing the moving module with the fixed one.
prac.relacionar_la_geometria_solar: Relate solar geometry to module orientation.
prac.operar_un_posicionador_remoto: Operate a remote positioner within safe limits.
prac.comparar_simultaneamente_un_sistema: Compare a fixed system and an orientable one simultaneously.
prac.cuantificar_perdidas_o_ganancias: Quantify losses or gains due to orientation.
prac.distinguir_variaciones_geometricas_: Distinguish geometric variations from environmental ones.
prac.anota_la_posicion_del: Note the position of the Sun (top bar: elevation and azimuth). Which way should module B be pointed?
prac.un_modulo_capta_mas: A module captures more when its normal points at the Sun: azimuth ≈ solar azimuth and tilt ≈ zenith angle.
prac.calibra_el_par_deja: Calibrate the pair: leave module B the same as A (azimuth 180°, tilt 17°) with MPPT load and wait for it to settle.
prac.dos_modulos_identicos_nunca: Two "identical" modules are never exactly identical. With the same orientation, the P_B/P_A ratio is your baseline and is used to correct the rest.
prac.barrido_de_azimut_con: AZIMUTH sweep: with the tilt at 17°, place B at no fewer than 4 different azimuths (e.g. 120°, 150°, 210°, 240°), waiting at each one until the point is recorded.
prac.la_tabla_de_abajo: The table below fills itself when the tracker stops and the power stays stable for 10 s. Choose the values yourself: your judgment decides which ones are worth measuring.
prac.el_azimut_esta_inmovilizado: The azimuth is locked ("Tilt only" mode): choose "Two axes" or "Azimuth only" in the Tracker panel.
prac.barrido_de_inclinacion_con: TILT sweep: with the azimuth at 180°, try at least 4 tilts (0°, 20°, 40°, 60°, 80°).
prac.mide_cuanto_pesa_la: Measure how much tilt matters compared with azimuth for this date and latitude.
prac.la_inclinacion_esta_inmovilizada: The tilt is locked ("Azimuth only" mode): choose "Two axes" or "Tilt only" in the Tracker panel.

prac.es_el_maximo_teorico: It is the "theoretical maximum" of the two-axis system for this time.
prac.en_que_orientacion_fue: At which orientation was the P_B/P_A ratio highest, and how does it compare with the position of the Sun? What part of the difference could be due to the environment rather than to geometry?

prac.p1_rub_1: I interpret Voc, Isc, Pmax, FF and η from my own sweep.
prac.p1_rub_2: I explain with data how Isc, Voc and Pmax change when irradiance drops.
prac.p1_rub_3: My calculations match those of my run, or I explain why they differ.
prac.p1_pred_text: Predict before measuring: how will Isc, Voc and Pmax change if irradiance drops sharply (clouds from 10 % to 60 %)?
prac.p1_pred_why: Predicting first and comparing afterwards is what best helps correct prior ideas: if you are wrong, the simulator will show you with your own data.
prac.p1_pred_q: Write your prediction with approximate numbers: by how much (in %) do you think each of Isc, Voc and Pmax will drop (or rise)? Why?
prac.p1_calc_text: With the data from your sweep calculate the fill factor FF = Pmax / (Voc · Isc) and the efficiency η = Pmax / (G · A), and check them against your run.
prac.p1_calc_why: FF and η summarize the quality of the module in one number. Calculating them yourself, rather than reading them, fixes what each variable measures.
prac.p1_calc_status: Your sweep: Pmax {pmax} W · Voc {voc} V · Isc {isc} A · G {g} W/m² · module area {area} m²
prac.p1_nubes_text: Raise the clouds to 60 % or more with the slider, wait a few seconds for G to settle and repeat the I‑V sweep.
prac.p1_nubes_ok: Second sweep recorded: G went from {g1} to {g2} W/m².
prac.p1_nubes_falta: Reference sweep: G = {g} W/m². The second one must have at least 15 % less irradiance. Sweeps done: {n}.
prac.p1_interp_text: Calculate Isc/G (in mA per W/m²) for your two sweeps and answer the question.
prac.p1_interp_why: If Isc/G comes out almost the same, Isc is proportional to irradiance: this is the basis of measuring irradiance with a reference cell.
prac.p1_q2: Compare your two sweeps: what happened to Isc/G, to Voc and to the efficiency η when irradiance dropped? Does it match your prediction? If not, which idea changed?
prac.p1_rep_s2: Second sweep {id}: G = {g} W/m², Pmax = {pmax} W, Isc = {isc} A, Voc = {voc} V, Isc/G = {iscg} mA per W/m², η = {eta} %.
prac.p1_pred_ref: Your two sweeps (G from {g1} to {g2} W/m²): Isc {i1} → {i2} A ({di}), Voc {v1} → {v2} V ({dv}), Pmax {p1} → {p2} W ({dp}). Compare with your prediction: Isc follows G almost proportionally, Voc barely changes (it depends on the logarithm of G) and Pmax falls almost as much as Isc.
prac.p1_q2_ref: Isc/G was {k1} and {k2} mA per W/m²: almost equal, because Isc is proportional to G. Voc changed {dv}: it depends only on the logarithm of G, and module temperature also matters. G changed {dg} and Pmax {dp}: Pmax falls almost as much as G (the fill factor improves slightly at lower current), so η went from {e1} % to {e2} %, that is, it changes little.
prac.p1_pred_expect: After the second sweep you will be able to compare your prediction with your data.
prac.p1_pred_evid: Prediction saved (it cannot be edited) and compared with your two sweeps.
prac.p1_pred_h1: An approximate number is worth more than “drops a lot”: write a percentage for each one.
prac.p1_pred_h2: There is no bad prediction: it is there to be compared with your data afterwards.
prac.p1_calc_expect: FF close to 0.75 and η close to 18 % in full sun (model values).
prac.p1_calc_evid: The FF and η you entered, checked against your sweep.
prac.p1_calc_h1: FF = Pmax / (Voc · Isc). Use the values on the “Your sweep” line.
prac.p1_calc_h2: η = Pmax / (G · A), with G in W/m² and A in m²; multiply by 100 to get %.
prac.p1_nubes_evid: Second sweep saved with its irradiance.
prac.p1_nubes_h2: The simulator’s clouds vary over time: wait for G to settle before sweeping.
prac.p1_interp_expect: Isc/G almost the same in both sweeps; Voc almost the same; η changes little.
prac.p1_interp_evid: Isc/G of both sweeps checked and question answered.
prac.p1_interp_h1: Isc/G = Isc (in mA) divided by G (in W/m²).
prac.p1_interp_h2: Also compare Voc of the two sweeps: what percentage changed?
prac.p2_rub_1: I relate the orientation that gives the most power to the position of the Sun.
prac.p2_rub_2: I quantify in % what is gained or lost relative to the baseline.
prac.p2_rub_3: I distinguish what is due to geometry from what is due to the environment or to measurement.
prac.p2_pred_text: Predict before measuring: which orientation will give module B the most power relative to A, and how much more?
prac.p2_pred_why: If you first estimate where the Sun is and how much the angle matters, you can later judge whether your measurements are reasonable.
prac.p2_pred_q: With the 11:00 Sun, which azimuth and tilt do you think will give the highest ratio P_B/P_A, and how many % above your baseline? Which will be the worst orientation you try and how many % worse?
prac.p2_calc_text: With your table calculate how much P_B/P_A changed at your best and at your worst point relative to the baseline (in %) and answer the question.
prac.p2_calc_why: The ratio with A removes the effect of clouds, wind and temperature, which affect both modules equally; what remains is geometry and measurement noise.
prac.p2_calc_status: Baseline: P_B/P_A = {base} · points in your table: {n}
prac.p2_f_best: Change of the best point relative to the baseline
prac.p2_f_worst: Change of the worst point relative to the baseline
prac.p2_pred_ref: Your best point was {hi} ({dhi} relative to the baseline) and your worst {lo} ({dlo}). Compare with your prediction of orientation and percentage.
prac.p2_q1_ref: Best manual point: {best}. Sun when we measured it: azimuth {saz}°, elevation {sel}°. The cos θ ratio (B relative to A) was {rc} and your power ratio corrected by the baseline, {rp}. They are similar because almost all the power comes from direct irradiance, which follows the cosine law; when the plane points far from the Sun, the real power is somewhat higher than the cosine predicts, because diffuse and reflected light do not depend on the angle in the same way. Since A and B are measured at the same time, wind, temperature and clouds affect both equally; that is why the ratio is used rather than absolute power. Part of the remaining difference is measurement noise (see σ in your table).
prac.p2_pred_expect: After the table you will see your best and worst points to compare.
prac.p2_pred_evid: Prediction saved and compared with your best and worst point.
prac.p2_pred_h1: Think about where the Sun is at that time: the simulator shows it in the top bar.
prac.p2_pred_h2: Write numbers (for example “+3 %”), even approximate ones.
prac.p2_calc_expect: The best point is close to the Sun’s azimuth (about 150–160° at this hour) and the worst in the most distant orientations.
prac.p2_calc_evid: Change of the best and worst point calculated and checked against your table; question answered.
prac.p2_calc_h1: Change % = (ratio of the point / ratio of the baseline − 1) × 100.
prac.p2_calc_h2: The ratio of each point is in the P_B/P_A column of your table; the baseline is the one at 180°/17°.
prac.p3_rub_1: I calculate the energy gain and the net gain from my runs.
prac.p3_rub_2: I explain why the gain changes with cloudiness.
prac.p3_rub_3: I support a recommendation with gain, consumption, complexity and maintenance.
prac.p3_pred_text: Predict before running: how much extra energy does two-axis tracking give, and what happens if the day is very cloudy?
prac.p3_pred_why: It is the real design question: is the tracker worth it at a cloudy site? Predicting makes you commit to an idea that you then compare with the data.
prac.p3_pred_q: In a clear sky, how many % more energy do you think two-axis tracking gives than the fixed module? And with 60 % clouds, will the gain be larger, equal or smaller, and why?
prac.p3_r3_text: RUN 3: two-axis astronomical tracking with 60 % clouds. Press “Prepare run (two axes, cloudy)” and let it run until 17:30.
prac.p3_r3_why: Same day, wind and seed as the previous runs; only the cloudiness changes. So the difference in gain is due to the clouds.
prac.p3_r4_text: RUN 4: sensor-based tracking with 60 % clouds (same cloudy scenario).
prac.p3_r4_why: With clouds the sensor can lose the signal. Watch how many minutes it spends without signal and what it costs in energy.
prac.p3_calc_text: With the run table calculate the energy gain of two-axis astronomical tracking, E_B/E_A − 1, in a clear sky and with 60 % clouds, and answer the question.
prac.p3_calc_why: Calculating it yourself, from the Wh, shows you what “gain” means and why it depends on the sky.
prac.p3_q1: Explain with your numbers why the gain changed between the clear and the cloudy sky, and what that implies for choosing a tracker at a site with many clouds.
prac.p3_decide_text: Close the comparison: with the four runs complete, decide which strategy you would recommend.
prac.p3_decide_why: A technical recommendation combines gain, motor consumption, complexity and maintenance, not just energy.
prac.p3_pred_ref: Your two-axis runs: gain {ga} with {ca} % clouds and {gc} with {cc} % clouds. Compare with your prediction: with clouds the fraction of diffuse light grows, and it reaches almost any orientation equally, so following the Sun adds less.
prac.p3_q1_ref: Gain in a clear sky {ga} and with clouds {gc}. The fixed module captured {ea} Wh in a clear sky and {ec} Wh with clouds. With clouds the direct light is reduced and the diffuse light matters more, and it reaches almost any orientation equally; following the Sun adds less. Even so the gain does not disappear: deciding whether it pays for the cost of the tracker depends on the size of the installation and the climate of the site.
prac.p3_q2_sensor: With clouds, sensor-based tracking delivered {es} Wh and astronomical tracking {ea} Wh (almost the same), even though the sensor spent {ns} min without signal. In this model, when the sensor loses the signal it holds its position and the Sun moves little in that time, so it loses almost no energy; the model does not represent the poor tracking under diffuse light that can occur in real sensors, and that limitation has not been validated against a real bench. The practical difference between the two is in reliability (astronomical tracking does not depend on the sky) and cost, not in this energy.
prac.p3_sensor_expect: In this model sensor-based tracking delivers almost the same energy as astronomical tracking; note how many minutes it loses the signal.
prac.p3_pred_expect: When you finish the runs you will see your gains to compare with your prediction.
prac.p3_pred_evid: Prediction saved and compared with your runs.
prac.p3_pred_h1: Write numbers (for example “+30 %”): an estimate is worth more than “a lot”.
prac.p3_pred_h2: Think about which part of the light depends on orientation and which does not.
prac.p3_r3_expect: Gain clearly smaller than in a clear sky.
prac.p3_r3_evid: Complete run of the cloudy scenario (p3-nublado-v1) with E_A, E_B, motors and gains.
prac.p3_r4_expect: Almost the same energy as cloudy astronomical tracking, with several minutes without sensor signal.
prac.p3_r4_evid: Complete cloudy run with sensors and minutes without signal.
prac.p3_calc_expect: The gain with clouds is much smaller than in a clear sky.
prac.p3_calc_evid: Gains calculated and checked against your two runs; question answered.
prac.p3_calc_h1: Gain % = (E_B / E_A − 1) × 100, with the Wh from the run table.
prac.p3_calc_h2: Use the “Astronomical · 2 axes” rows of the two skies.
prac.p3_decide_expect: A recommendation that mentions net gain, consumption, complexity and maintenance.
prac.p3_decide_h1: Compare the net gain against complexity: how many points of gain justify one more moving part?
prac.p3_decide_h2: Remember what you saw with clouds and with the sensor state.
prac.p4_goal: Quantify how reliable the laboratory data are: repeatability of a measurement, outliers, gaps, a miscalibrated sensor and how uncertainties combine. The uncertainty figures are illustrative of the model, not those of the real bench (still pending calibration).
prac.p4_ilo_1: Quantify the repeatability of a measurement with the mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation.
prac.p4_ilo_2: Detect outliers and gaps in a data series and decide how to treat them.
prac.p4_ilo_3: Identify a miscalibrated sensor and estimate its correction factor.
prac.p4_ilo_4: Combine relative uncertainties to estimate the uncertainty of the efficiency.
prac.p4_ilo_5: Judge which laboratory conclusions are robust against uncertainty.
prac.p4_rub_1: I calculate the mean, standard deviation and CV of my repeated sweeps.
prac.p4_rub_2: I identify outliers, gaps and the factor of the miscalibrated sensor.
prac.p4_rub_3: I explain which conclusions withstand the uncertainty and which do not.
prac.p4_pred_text: Predict before measuring: if you repeat the same I‑V sweep three times under the same conditions, how much will Pmax vary?
prac.p4_pred_why: Every measurement repeats with some scatter. Having a prior idea of its size lets you tell whether a result is surprising or just noise.
prac.p4_pred_q: How much do you think three Pmax values measured under the same conditions vary from each other (in %)? Would that variation matter more, or using a pyranometer with 5 % uncertainty when calculating efficiency?
prac.p4_rep_text: Run three I‑V sweeps in a row without changing clouds, time, orientation or mode (irradiance must stay within ±3 % between sweeps).
prac.p4_rep_why: Repeating the same measurement under the same conditions separates measurement noise from real changes.
prac.p4_repcalc_text: With the Pmax values of your valid sweeps calculate the mean, the sample standard deviation s and the coefficient of variation CV = s / mean.
prac.p4_repcalc_why: The CV is the relative repeatability: the figure you will compare with the effect you want to detect.
prac.p4_def_text: Review the teaching series in the table: 16 readings of G (pyranometer) and Isc with deliberately injected faults. Count the outlier readings and the rows with no data, and calculate the factor k = (mean Isc/G of the good rows) / 13.0, with Isc/G in mA per W/m².
prac.p4_def_why: Real data come with faults: a momentary shadow, logger gaps, a miscalibrated sensor. Detecting them before averaging avoids false conclusions.
prac.p4_f_gap: Number of rows with no data (gaps)
prac.p4_q1: What would you do with the outliers and the gaps before averaging, and what would happen to the efficiency if you did not correct the pyranometer? What would you note in the report so another person can repeat your analysis?
prac.p4_unc_text: Estimate the relative uncertainty of the efficiency by combining the repeatability of Pmax (your CV) with that of the pyranometer: u(η)/η = √(CV² + u_G²), with u_G = 5 %, and answer the question.
prac.p4_unc_why: Independent uncertainties add in quadrature: the largest one dominates. Here you will see which one rules.
prac.p4_unc_status: Your CV = {cv} % · assumed u_G = {ug} % (illustrative; not the bench’s)
prac.p4_q2: Which of the two sources dominates the uncertainty of η? With that uncertainty, which conclusions from practices 1 to 3 remain firm and which could you not claim? Consider that the gain E_B/E_A is calculated from the electrical energies of two modules measured with the same chain.
prac.p4_seg_text: Optional: trigger a 20 m/s gust and watch the tracker go to the safe position on its own. The data from that period are not valid for analyzing normal capture: how would you flag them?
prac.p4_seg_why: Data quality includes knowing when the system was in an abnormal state. The wind protection lives in the controller and cannot be changed from the client.

prac.p4_rep_head: ## Quality and uncertainty (illustrative figures from the model)
prac.p4_rep_rep: Repeatability: {n} sweeps with G ≈ {g} W/m²; mean Pmax = {mean} W, s = {sd} W, CV = {cv} %.
prac.p4_rep_rep_no: Repeatability: 3 valid sweeps were not completed.
prac.p4_rep_data: Teaching series: outlier readings in rows {out}; gaps in rows {gap}; pyranometer factor k = {k}. Assumed pyranometer uncertainty: {ug} % (illustrative; the bench’s is pending).
prac.p4_pred_ref: With your {n} sweeps: mean Pmax {mean} W, s = {sd} W, CV = {cv} %. The repeatability of the sweep is a few tenths of a percent: much smaller than the {ug} % assumed for the pyranometer. That comparison decides which source of uncertainty dominates in η.
prac.p4_q1_ref: Outliers: rows {out} (Isc far below the trend, typical of a momentary shadow). They are flagged and excluded from the average, noting how many there were and why, without deleting them from the original file. Gaps: rows {gap}; they are not filled by inventing data, the gap is noted and the average is taken over what exists. Pyranometer: k = {k}, that is, the pyranometer reads about {pc} % low and, uncorrected, the efficiency would come out about {pc} % too high (it is divided by a G lower than the real one). Correct it with k or recalibrate the sensor, and note which of the two was done. In the report: which rows were excluded and why, which correction was applied and with what data.
prac.p4_q2_ref: u(η)/η ≈ {u} %: the pyranometer dominates ({ug} %), not the repeatability ({cv} %). With that uncertainty, two absolute efficiencies that differ by less than ≈ {u} % cannot be told apart. The gain E_B/E_A is calculated from the electrical energies of the two modules, without going through G; so the pyranometer uncertainty does not enter, and what matters is the A = B baseline (practice 2) and the scatter of the electrical measurement. A gain of 30 % is firm; one of 3 % holds only if you measured and subtracted the baseline.
prac.p4_q2_p3: In your practice 3, the gain with clouds was {g}: it is much larger than the repeatability ({cv} %), so it is a real effect, but check the baseline of A and B.
